title: The Metal Never Changed
logline: A cast-bronze figure about a thousand years old has been a god in a shrine on a cliff above the open ocean, then metal in the ground for three centuries with nobody saying anything to it, then an object a town council pulled out of a hole it was digging for water, then a god in a shrine again — and the alloy took the same weather all the way through.
human_question: If something I call by a name spent three hundred years being nothing that anybody named, and came back out of the ground and was named again, what exactly was the name resting on the whole time?

place.what_kind_of_place: A headland of hard bedded rock pushed out into the open ocean at the end of a long bay, with a cliff on its seaward side that goes straight down into deep water and a vertical cleft split clean through it that the swell runs into and out of. On the top, at the point, a busy Hindu temple: a gate tower, a courtyard, a colossal seated figure standing in the open air, stalls along the approach, and people arriving from half past five in the morning. The whole headland sits inside an eighteenth-century fort that is still a working army post, so the road up runs through a checkpoint and then a kilometre of ramparts, trees and tame spotted deer before it reaches the temple. And under the water at the foot of the cliff, in nowhere more than about fifteen feet, the sea bed is strewn with cut and squared blocks lying in no order at all.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off, and none of them exists anywhere else on this slate. The sun comes up out of the sea. Filmed from a boat standing off the point, the cliff goes from a black mass with no detail in it to a red wall in about four minutes, and the light arrives horizontally off open water rather than over a ridge. Then the cleft: a vertical slot cut the full height of the rock, wide enough to hold moving sea at the bottom of it, which can only be read properly from a boat and which the long lens cannot flatten. And then the descent, which is the film's payoff — over the side, the surface closing, the light going green, and four or five feet down a squared stone face with bands of sun crossing it and weed on every edge. It is the one shot in this group that has to be taken underwater, and it is also the clearest possible statement of what the film is saying: a worked stone with nothing on it to say what it was ever called.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Everything in the frame is water or weather and none of it is under the crew's control. Swell runs at the foot of the cliff all day and reverses the light in the cleft as it comes and goes. Wind gets up off the sea through the morning and takes the surface glass off, which closes the underwater work. Salt haze thickens as the sun climbs. The visibility in the water changes week to week and season to season. Ashore, the temple's own day opens at half past five, shuts in the middle of the day and opens again in the late afternoon, so the crowd on the headland doubles and empties twice. And the whole thing is governed by a season that decides whether the sea can be worked at all.
place.when_it_looks_best: First light, from the water, for the cliff. The east-coast dry season, roughly May to September, is the only window; April and May are reported to give the calmest sea and the best underwater visibility, of the order of fifteen to twenty-five metres. The north-east monsoon from about November to March puts a heavy sea onto this coast and most diving operations close. Middle of the day is useless: the cliff goes flat, the haze whites out the horizon and the water loses its shafts. The film also has to avoid the twenty-two-day festival period in April and the three-day procession after Sivarathri, when the headland is full and a camera is least welcome.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A sea film with a clean shape: dark water to bright water, above to below and back. It starts on a flat black sea an hour before dawn with a rock standing in it, waits for the sun to come up out of the ocean and set the cliff alight, works along the face and into the cleft from a boat, goes over the side and down onto a floor of cut stone, comes back up through the light, walks ashore into a loud bright morning on top of the headland, and ends on nothing but open water and wind. Someone who never hears a word of it gets a complete piece with a descent, a discovery and a return.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a piece of bookkeeping. The voice never argues and never corrects anybody: it lists what happened to one piece of cast metal, in order, with the dates, and lets the list do the work. In a shrine. In the ground, unaddressed, for three centuries. Out of a hole dug for water, described by weight in an alloy. In a shrine again. What the sources separate — the name, and whatever the name is laid on — this history has already separated and put back together, without anybody intending to demonstrate anything. And the film stops exactly where the sources stop: it observes that the two come apart, and it takes no position at all on what the name refers to.

sequence.on_screen: An hour before sunrise, from a small boat standing off the point on a flat sea. The headland is a black mass with no detail in it; the only light in the frame is a grey line behind it and the wake. Then the sun comes up out of open water and the cliff goes from black to red in about four minutes.
sequence.voice: At the top of that rock there is a figure of cast bronze, believed to be about a thousand years old: Shiva seated, with Parvati. It stands in a shrine and people come to it every morning. It has also spent three centuries lying in the ground about five hundred yards from where it is now, with nobody anywhere saying a word to it. The alloy is the same alloy. What changed was the name it was carrying and what people did in front of it, and the books this series is about keep those two things in separate columns.

sequence.on_screen: Full sunrise on the cliff, still from the water: a wall of bedded rock running straight down into the swell, and the cleft in it — a vertical slot the full height of the face with sea moving at the bottom of it. The boat holds off; the camera is low and the swell lifts the frame and drops it.
sequence.voice: On the Tamil New Year, in the early 1620s — the accounts do not agree on the year — a Portuguese force under Constantino de Sá de Noronha took the temple that stood up there. The accounts say some of the soldiers came in dressed as priests. The accounts say the building was levered over this edge into the sea, and its cut stone went into the fort that is still standing on the same headland. And the accounts suppose that before that, some of the metal figures were carried off and put into the ground. Those are entries in a record. This film is not a verdict on any of them.

sequence.on_screen: Over the side. The surface closes and the light turns green. Four or five feet down, on a bottom nowhere more than about fifteen feet deep, squared blocks lie in every direction, weeded and barnacled, with bands of sun travelling across them as the swell passes. A long hold on one cut face. If diving is not permitted, the same ground from the surface on a glass morning, looking straight down through clear water.
sequence.voice: In 1956 two divers working about two hundred yards off this headland, Arthur C. Clarke and Mike Wilson, worked out that the blocks underneath them were not the sea's doing. They found the capital of a doorway, and a broken column with a lotus-petal design cut into every face of its square ends. Nothing down here is labelled. These books define the physical side of the world as whatever gets struck and altered by what opposes it, and the pair they name for that is cold against heat. Salt water is doing it to this, steadily, and it has never needed to know what any of it was for.

sequence.on_screen: Rising slowly. The blocks fall away underneath, the green goes pale, and the surface comes down as a moving silver ceiling and breaks. Then a single held frame back down the water column at the whole scattered floor of stone, small and far off.
sequence.voice: And these books will not let the bottom of the world be made of lumps. What is finally there, they say, is not stones and clods of clay but forces — and forces have no length of their own, no shortness, no roundness, no squareness. A great quantity of them gathering is what gets the power to show you a tree, a rock, a hill, a body. It looks like substance. It is the altered condition of an enormous amount of activity. Every straight edge down here is ours.

sequence.on_screen: Ashore and inland, off the rock altogether: flat ordinary ground a few hundred yards back from the sea. A street edge, dry earth, a standpipe, a wall, the hard flat light of nine in the morning and not a scrap of sea in the frame. Held long enough to be boring.
sequence.voice: In 1950 the town's urban council was digging for water a few hundred yards back from the rock, and struck metal about a yard down. Three figures came out, better than a hundred pounds' weight of gold and copper alloy; two more had come out some months earlier and nobody official had been told. Every word of that is a description of an object. For three hundred years nobody in the world was saying a name at this metal. Then somebody was again. The books keep the name in one column and whatever the name is laid on in the other, and they are serious enough about it to sort names into six kinds according to how the one stands to the other.

sequence.on_screen: The headland from the landward side in full morning: the gate, the road climbing through the fort under trees, spotted deer on the verge, stalls, then the temple wall and the tower standing against an enormous flat sea. No shrine interior. No worship. No face. The camera stays outside and waits.
sequence.voice: They were carried round the district and put back, and the rebuilt shrine opened on the third of March 1963. A three-day procession has gone out after Sivarathri every year since the year after they came up. So: a figure in a shrine; metal in the ground; an object handed over by weight to the authorities; a figure in a shrine. Four situations and one alloy. I am not going to tell you what the name refers to. These books do not, and no camera is going to settle it. What they say is narrower and stranger. The sound of a word is a real event in the air. The name that sound carries is a different item from the sound, and it lives in whoever is listening.

sequence.on_screen: From the cliff top at the point, looking out. Nothing in the frame but open water to the horizon and the wind coming straight onto the rock; a railing going in and out of focus. Then back down the face to the waterline and a long hold on the swell arriving.
sequence.voice: These books say the physical side of the world is the part that gets altered by whatever opposes it. They count four things as finally real. Three of them are made, and they come apart. The fourth is not made by anything at all, and it is the one thing here I can name and cannot show you; it is not this, and it is not the sea either. What can be shown is a piece of metal that has been called several things and called nothing, and has taken the same weather either way.

concept_merge.why_together: C084 is the whole engine and this history is its case rather than its illustration. The Pradeepika defines paññatti as the convention other than mind and matter, so called both because it is made known and because it makes known [C084-P:L25], and the Mārgaya opens by saying that most of what appears to people as the things of the world is paññatti, and that learning to recognise it is what lets the ultimate be picked out cleanly [C084-M:L5]. The Mārgaya then separates the two classes the film lives on: the meaning-concept is whatever rises in the hearer's mind by way of the word [C084-M:L9], and the name-concept is the name that raises it, with the explicit warning that the sound and the name are not the same item, because the sound is an ultimate and the name is not [C084-M:L21]. The Pradeepika puts the same thing structurally: a name-concept is whatever designates either the ultimates or the eight concepts [C084-P:L47], and it then sorts names by whether the name and the basis it rests on are ultimately there [C084-P:L51; C084-P:L55], as the Mārgaya does at greater length with its six kinds [C084-M:L23]. That sorting is the point: it is only possible because the name and the basis are already being counted as two items. A cast figure is also, in the sources' own terms, a quantity of substance gathered and joined [C084-M:L15] standing in a shape [C084-M:L13] — the same family as the collective concepts the Pradeepika lists, the ground, mountains, rivers and the sea [C084-P:L29]. C002 supplies what the camera is actually looking at while that is being said. Both sources define materiality by what opposing conditions such as cold and heat do to it [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], which is exactly what happened to this alloy: melted to be made and three centuries in earth. And both refuse to let the ultimates be substances — not visible to the eye, not counted as substance, mere activity, a kind of force, and in the same breath true, existent and indivisible [C002-P:L34]; not lumps like stones or clods of clay but forces, and therefore without length, shortness, smallness, largeness, roundness or squareness of their own [C002-M:L3] — while allowing that masses of them gathering get the power to show forth trees, stones, hills and bodies, which looks like substance and is the altered condition of a collection of activities [C002-P:L40]. Put on one buried and recovered bronze, the two digests produce a film that can say precisely what changed and precisely what did not, without once saying what the name refers to.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the separability of a name from its basis is not a thought experiment here; it was performed, by accident, over more than three hundred and twenty years, and then undone. Almost every treatment of this idea has to stage it — divide the cloth, take the table apart — and the staging is what makes it feel like a trick. Nobody staged this. A shrine was taken and the metal, the accounts suppose, was hidden; the metal lay in the ground while the name it had carried went on being used by people who had no idea where the metal was; a council looking for water met it at a yard down and weighed it; and then the name was put back on. Four situations, one alloy, and the alloy registered only the things C002 says materiality registers. C084 alone would make this a film about vocabulary. C002 alone would make it a film about corrosion. Together they also close the two exits the site makes available. The cheap one is 'so it was only metal all along', which the sources do not license: the digest's own bar is that a film must never tell a participant that the name they use is wrong, the existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories and not a scheme of true and false, and C002 keeps the ultimates fully real and the conventional world valid in its own domain. The other exit is grievance, and the material forbids that too, because the argument the film is making runs identically whichever way the history had gone.

concept_links.why: Everything the film claims is in this digest. Paññatti is the convention other than mind and matter, named for being made known and for making known [C084-P:L25]; the Mārgaya's opening says that most of what appears as the things of the world is paññatti and that recognising it is what allows the ultimate to be separated out cleanly [C084-M:L5]; the meaning-concept is what rises in the hearer's mind by way of the word [C084-M:L9]; the name-concept is the name that designates either the ultimates or the eight concepts [C084-P:L47]; and the sound is emphatically not the name, because the sound is an ultimate and the name it conveys is not [C084-M:L21]. The sixfold sorting of name-concepts [C084-M:L23], and the Pradeepika's two worked cases of it [C084-P:L51; C084-P:L55], are cited here for one reason only: a scheme that classifies names by how they stand to their basis is a scheme that already counts the name and the basis as two items. That is the whole of the film's argument, and this location supplies a documented instance of the two coming apart and going back together. The digest's three limits are load-bearing and are built into the writing rather than appended to it. The film never tells anybody that the name they use for this figure is wrong, and beat six says out loud that it takes no position on what the name refers to. It never sorts this particular case into one of the six kinds, because doing so would be exactly the adjudication the digest forbids. It never treats the existent and non-existent pairs as 'true' and 'false' names, because they are technical Abhidhamma categories. And it never slides into 'language constructs reality' or 'nothing is real', because the sources keep the ultimates fully real and conventional wholes valid in their own domain. Where the film does use the collective and shape families — a quantity of substance gathered and joined [C084-M:L15], standing in an arrangement [C084-M:L13], of the same family as the ground, mountains, rivers and the sea [C084-P:L29] — it is describing what a cast object is, not ranking it.

C002 answers the question the first beat raises and the camera cannot: what is the thing that did not change? Both sources define materiality as what is struck and altered by opposing conditions such as cold and heat [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], and that is the exact register in which this alloy has had a life — cast by heat and buried in earth for three centuries. Both also refuse the picture of the ultimates as stuff: not visible to the eye, not counted as substance, mere activity, a kind of force, and in the same sentence true, existent and indivisible [C002-P:L34]; not lumps like stones or clods of clay but forces, and so lacking length, shortness, smallness, largeness, roundness and squareness of their own [C002-M:L3]. The fourth beat is that second sentence filmed, because the squared face of a submerged block is the most obviously manufactured thing on the sea bed and the sources put squareness on the far side of the line; and the Pradeepika's own concession — that masses of these gathering get the power to show forth trees, stones, hills and bodies, which appears as substance and is the altered condition of a collection of activities [C002-P:L40] — is what keeps that beat from becoming a debunking. The digest's does-not-transfer lines set the film's edges directly. The extract only names the four great elements and does not define them [C002-P:L40], so the voice never glosses the sea, the rock, the sun or the wind as water, earth, fire and air, which is the standing temptation of a coastal location. 'Everything is energy' is ruled out, because the forces-not-substances claim is a precise analytic point inside a fourfold scheme. 'Nothing is real' and 'it is all illusion' are ruled out in the same line that calls the ultimates true and existent. And the fourth reality — not produced by causes, free of birth, ageing and death, object of supramundane knowledge and realised by noble ones [C002-P:L42; C002-P:L46], free of the fires of defilement and of suffering, always present, reached only through great effort on the supramundane path [C002-M:L21] — is the one place the digest asks for an expert reading before anything is spoken. The last beat therefore touches it in a single sentence, says it cannot be shown, says that neither the metal nor the sea is it, and stops; it is written to be cut back rather than expanded if the check goes against it.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a name and the thing a name is laid on are two items, and that you can watch them come apart and go back together without anything having to be proved. The demonstration is a list of dates and a piece of metal: in a shrine, in the ground, in a council's hands by weight, in a shrine. Nothing on screen is shown to be unreal and nobody's name for anything is corrected. What is shown is that the alloy took the weather — heat, earth — and took nothing else at all, and that everything else in the story happened in people.
what_must_be_real: A living, busy temple and a working army post, filmed as they are on the day. No act of worship is interrupted, restarted, repeated, arranged or lit for filming, and no puja is filmed at all. No priest, worshipper or visitor is an exhibit, is presented as devout or observant, is used as a figure for scale, or appears without consent given in their own language; nobody who cannot meaningfully refuse a camera is in frame. If filming the bronzes is refused — which should be the expectation — the film is made without them and says nothing that depends on having seen them. Nothing is moved, cleaned, wetted, lifted or repositioned above or below the water, and no object is touched on the sea bed. The film records the layers of this place and adjudicates none of them: no community is cast as a destroyer and none as a victim, the date is stated as a date, no faction is named, the war is not filmed and is not used as atmosphere, and nothing is narrated as anyone's grievance or anyone's due. Competing claims about the site's age, origins and earlier custody are recorded as competing and are never settled on screen or in narration. No uniform, no checkpoint, no serving personnel and no closed area is filmed. Every date, weight and measurement in the voice is stated no more confidently than the sources state it, and where the accounts disagree — as they do about the year, the number of figures and the circumstances — the disagreement is either stated or left out, never smoothed.
position_hint: Late in the group, and after at least one film has already taken a name off a thing, so that the four situations read as an observation rather than a provocation. It is the only film in the group with water at its centre and the only one that can go below the surface, so it also wants to sit away from the other cliff-and-height material. It is the group's most politically exposed location and the one that most needs the rest of the series to have established that this voice records and does not judge. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Adjudicating. This is the largest risk on the slate. A colonial power destroyed a temple of a living community on that community's new year, and the district was heavily affected by the war. The film states what is recorded, keeps the contested things in what_is_disputed, names no faction, and narrates nothing as grievance, as progress or as anyone's due. The C084 digest's bar that a film must never tell a participant the name they use is wrong applies to every name this headland has had.

A live naming dispute. The headland is subject to a current Hindu–Buddhist claim: some Sinhala Buddhist writers identify it with a Buddhist monastery named in the chronicles, and the argument is still being made in print (for example a LankaWeb polemic of April 2024). A film about a name coming off something and being put back on can be heard as taking a side on what this site should be called or whose it is. The voice never enters that dispute, never names either claim, never implies that any name for the headland or the shrine is the original, the correct or the restored one, and never lets 'the name was put back' stand for anything but the documented reinstallation of these bronzes. The competing claims are recorded as layers in what_is_disputed and never adjudicated.

Arguing that the figure is 'only metal'. The sources do not license it, the digest forbids telling anyone their name is wrong, and the existent and non-existent pairs are technical categories rather than a scheme of true and false. The film observes that a name and its basis are separable; it takes no position on what the name refers to, and beat six says so in the narration so the position cannot be inferred.

Memorial and legacy framing. C061's bar is live and this site invites the breach constantly: no shot or line may read as 'what was left behind', as remembrance, or as loss. The claim the film makes is about a name and a piece of metal, not about mourning a building.

Using the war, or the ruin under the water, as spectacle. No wreck-as-elegy grade, no faction, no damage composed for pathos, and the submerged stone is filmed because it is evidence the film needs and for no other reason.
Overreaching into 'nothing is real'. The sources call the ultimates true, existent and indivisible and keep conventional wholes valid in their own domain.
Overreaching into 'everything is energy'. The forces-not-substances claim is a precise analytic point inside a fourfold scheme, not a statement about vibrations.

Glossing the sea, the rock, the sun and the wind as water, earth, fire and air. The extract names the four great elements and does not define them, and a coastal location makes this the easiest mistake in the film.

Misparaphrasing the fourth reality in the last beat, or letting an empty horizon imply it without saying anything. The digest calls the wording subtle and asks for an expert check before any narration touches it; that beat is written to be checked and to be cut back rather than expanded.

Filming the bronzes at all. Photography inside shrines is frequently prohibited here and permission should be assumed refused until it is granted in writing. The film is built so that the figures are described and never shown, and beat six is composed from outside the shrine.

Filming inside a working military installation. The headland carries an army base and the approach passes a checkpoint; uniforms, gates and closed areas must never enter a frame, and the crew should expect its equipment to be inspected.

Drone. Treat refusal as the default. Any flight needs Civil Aviation Authority registration and Defence Ministry clearance, military installations are no-fly, and this is a naval town as well as an army post. The film is written so that no beat needs an aerial: everything wide comes from a boat, and everything high comes from the cliff top.

The underwater beats depend on two separate permissions and on the weather. Diving here is an established recreational activity, but this sea bed is an archaeological context and the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund's Maritime Archaeology Unit are the authorities for it, not a dive shop. Nothing may be touched, moved or lifted. If diving is refused, the fallback is surface and over-the-side work on a glass morning, because the masonry is reported at about five feet in water nowhere more than fifteen; if that fails too, beats three and four have to be rebuilt at the waterline and the film loses its best shot.

Season and sea state. The window is roughly May to September, the north-east monsoon closes the water from about November to March, and a single week of wind can cost the whole underwater sequence. There is no second take.
Becoming a history film. The dates are the argument, but this is a film about a cliff, a sea and a piece of metal. If the voice is explaining more than it is pointing, the balance has gone.

Colliding with the group's fort film. That one owns reused building material — carved pre-colonial stone inside later walls. The stones of this temple also went into a fort, and that fact appears here once, in a single clause in beat two, and is never the subject and never the payoff.
drop_if: The film can only be made by filming worship, by filming inside a shrine against the temple's wishes, or by putting a camera on people who have come to worship.
Neither diving nor surface work over the submerged stone can be permitted or safely done, so beats three and four have nothing on screen and the film's payoff does not exist.
Filming on the headland cannot be done without capturing serving personnel, checkpoints or closed areas.
The temple or the community makes it clear that a film of this kind is unwelcome at this site, in which case there is no version of it worth making.

connections.note: Kept deliberately apart. That film owns reused building material: a fort whose walls hold stone cut for older buildings. This one is about a name coming off a piece of metal and going back on, and the reuse of this temple's stone appears in exactly one clause. If this film drifts towards recycled masonry it has become the other one.
Four names alive at once on one mountain, all of them being used; and one name that was not being used by anybody for three centuries and then was again. The same separation, from opposite ends.

Two sites where the record will not settle what it is looking at. There the dispute is about a legend the stones contradict; here it is about a date, a count of figures and the age of a shrine, and in both cases the film's job is to keep the dispute a dispute.

selection.reason: It is the group's Hindu film and its only sea film, and the concept is not carried by resemblance but by a documented sequence of events in which a name and its basis came apart for three centuries and were put back together. It is also the only film on the slate that can go underwater.

review.note: Confirmed by Chathura on 2026-09-25, after his own hand-edits to this record, and reset to pending on 2026-09-26 because a GRP-01 audit corrected voice lines; under standing decision 9 a change to what the voice says invalidates the verdict, so the film needs judging again. The location, the concepts, the structure and his wording are otherwise unchanged. The changes are these. Beat one: 'a little over a thousand years old' became 'believed to be about a thousand years old', because Clarke's 'about the 10th century' is a stylistic attribution and no scientific date is known. Beat two: 'On the fourteenth of April 1622' became 'On the Tamil New Year, in the early 1620s — the accounts do not agree on the year', because Clarke gives Hindu New Year's Day 1624 while the reference account's 1622 rests on Lach; 'The accounts say' now stands before the levering over the edge, which is attested here only through Rasanayagam (1926); and the burial of the metal figures is now 'the accounts suppose', because Clarke's own word is 'must have' — an inference from where the bronzes were found. Beat five: 'two more had come out of the same ground' became 'two more had come out', because Clarke does not say where they were found. Beat seven: the sentence 'The salt is on the bronze up here too, every morning' was cut, because it is unsourced and the bronzes are inside a shrine; the matching salt clauses in the concept fields went with it. In the research: the disguise, the looting, the killing, the levering and the burial moved from what_is_certain to what_is_disputed with their earliest attestations named, and the unsourced claim that the disguise descends from seventeenth-century chronicle tradition was withdrawn; the two dates are recorded side by side; a risk now guards the live Hindu–Buddhist identification dispute over the headland, which the voice must never enter; and the evidence note now says the location was proposed by Claude. Still unverified: nothing has been traced to a seventeenth-century Portuguese or Tamil primary text, Rasanayagam's page was not read directly, the commander's name rests on the reference account alone, and one point in the audit brief was itself wrong — Clarke does report the disguise, the looting and, as 'probably', the killing — which is recorded in the research note.

suggested_location.region: Trincomalee District, Eastern Province — at the end of the headland east of Trincomalee town, inside Fort Frederick, with the open ocean on the seaward side and the inner harbour behind
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place where the concept is a sequence of dated events rather than a resemblance, and where the register is unlike anything else on the slate. The argument the film needs is that a name and the thing the name is laid on are separate items, and this site performed that separation by accident and then reversed it: a cast bronze believed, on style, to be of about the tenth century stood in a shrine, is supposed to have been buried when the temple was destroyed in the early 1620s, and lay in the ground for three centuries while the name it had carried went on being used, was struck by a council digging a water well in 1950 and handed over as a hundred-odd pounds of gold and copper alloy, and was carried back and reinstalled in 1963. Four situations, one alloy. Nothing had to be staged and nothing has to be argued. The second half of the concept is under the water: the building that was pushed off this cliff is on the sea bed at about five feet, and a squared block down there with sun crossing it is a worked thing with nothing on it to say what it was ever called. And the place films like nowhere else in the group. It is the only location with the sun coming up out of open water, the only vertical sea cliff, the only cleft, and the only site that can be shot from a boat and from below the surface. It is also the group's Hindu film and its only Eastern Province film, which is why it exists.
what_to_film: The headland before sunrise from a boat standing off the point: a black mass on a flat sea with no detail in it, then the sun coming up out of open water and the cliff turning over from black to red. This is the opening and it is a four-minute window on a clear morning.

The cliff face from the water in the first hour, long and slow along the bedding, with the swell lifting the camera; and the cleft, which reads only from a boat, filmed from far enough back to hold its whole height and close enough to see the sea running into the bottom of it.
The same cleft from above, from the temple side, looking straight down the slot into moving water.

Underwater, if it can be permitted and safely done: the floor of cut and squared blocks at four or five feet on a bottom nowhere more than about fifteen, weeded and barnacled, with bands of sun travelling over them. One long static hold on a single worked face is the film's payoff shot. Nothing is touched, moved or lifted.
The ascent through the water column, the silver ceiling breaking, and one held frame back down at the whole scattered floor of stone.

A surface-only version of both underwater beats for the likely case that diving is refused: over the side on a glass morning with a polariser, looking straight down through clear water at the same ground.

Flat ordinary ground a few hundred yards inland from the rock, with no sea in the frame at all — a street edge, dry earth, a standpipe, hard nine-o'clock light. This is beat five and it has to be deliberately dull.

The approach on the landward side: the road climbing through the fort under trees, spotted deer on the verge, stalls, and the temple wall and tower standing against a very large flat sea. No gate, no checkpoint, no uniform, no closed area in frame.

The exterior of the shrine only, in the ordinary working morning, with no puja and no worshipper in focus; the colossal seated figure in the open air is exterior and may be filmable where the shrines are not.
From the cliff top at the point: nothing but open water to the horizon, the wind coming straight onto the rock, and a long hold at the waterline on the swell arriving. This is the close.
The bronzes themselves only if the temple grants it in writing and on its own terms, and the film is built to work entirely without them.
suggested_location.access: The temple stands at the seaward end of the headland inside Fort Frederick, which is an active Sri Lanka Army post. Visitors enter through the fort gate, where identification is checked, and go about a kilometre up a public road through the fort, past ramparts, trees, spotted deer and a line of stalls, to the temple at the point; parts of the fort are military and closed. The temple is reported open daily from about 05:30 to 12:30 and again from about 16:30 to 20:30, which puts sunrise inside opening hours. Shoes are removed in the inner precincts and modest dress is required. Photography inside shrines is frequently prohibited and photography during puja should be assumed refused; photography restrictions also apply within the military area of the fort. The sea below is reached by boat from the town's bays, and the rock is an established recreational dive site with reported depths of about five to twenty-four metres, worked by operators in the April-to-September season. None of that constitutes permission to film: the submerged stone is an archaeological context, and the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund's Maritime Archaeology Unit are the authorities for anything done over it. Any unmanned flight needs Civil Aviation Authority registration and Defence Ministry clearance, military installations are no-fly, and refusal should be the planning assumption in a town that is also a major naval station. Every one of these arrangements is reported by secondary sources and is unverified.
suggested_location.best_time: Sunrise, and the east-coast dry season, roughly May to September. April and May are reported to give the calmest sea and the best underwater visibility, of the order of fifteen to twenty-five metres; the north-east monsoon from about November to March puts a heavy sea on this coast and most diving operations close. The first hour after sunrise is the whole of the film's light: it comes horizontally off open water onto a vertical face, and by mid-morning the cliff is flat and the haze has taken the horizon. The underwater work wants the same hour, before the wind gets up and takes the surface. The film should avoid the twenty-two-day chariot festival period in April around the Tamil New Year, and the three-day procession after Sivarathri: those are the days when the headland is fullest, when worship is most continuous, and when a camera is least appropriate.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, done with web search on 25 September 2026; nothing has been checked on the ground or against a printed edition. The 14 April 1622 date and Constantino de Sá de Noronha (cited there to Lach and Olsen), the soldiers entering dressed as Iyer priests, the structure being pushed over the cliff into the sea and fleeing priests burying statues (all three cited there to Rasanayagam 1926, p. 378), the use of the temple's stone for the fort on the same headland, the survival of processional images at the temple at Thampalakamam, the 1950 recovery by the town's urban council while digging a water well about five hundred yards from the site, the five named tenth-century bronzes, the reinstallation and the opening of the rebuilt shrine on 3 March 1963, the annual three-day procession after Sivarathri held every year since 1951, the twenty-two-day April chariot festival, the 1956 dive by Arthur C. Clarke and Mike Wilson and the recovery of the Swayambhu lingam are from the Wikipedia articles listed. The 1950 and 1956 detail is independently and much better sourced from Arthur C. Clarke's own signed account, 'Ceylon and the Underwater Archaeologist', Expedition Magazine 6, no. 3 (May 1964), read in full at the Penn Museum's digitised copy: the workmen striking metal about a yard down, three figures of better than a hundred pounds' weight of gold and copper alloy, two more unearthed months earlier without the authorities being told (he does not say where), the five statues then standing in the new temple, the doorway capital and the lotus-petal column, the water nowhere more than fifteen feet deep with most of the masonry about five feet down, and the site being about two hundred yards off the headland. Clarke's own dating of the destruction is 1624, not 1622, and that conflict is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than reconciled. The account of the Swayambhu lingam being found not in 1956 but in 1962, during filming, after repeated unsuccessful searches, is from the lakdiva reprint of a 1997 newspaper piece on Mike Wilson and directly contradicts the implication of the Wikipedia wording; both are recorded and neither is treated as settled. Dive depths, the season and the reported visibility are from recreational diving sources and are commercial descriptions, not survey data. Opening hours, the checkpoint, the dress code and the photography restrictions are from 2025 and 2026 visitor guides and change often. Drone practice is from the Civil Aviation Authority's own page and secondary summaries. The Maritime Archaeology Unit's remit is from the Central Cultural Fund and from published accounts of the Antiquities Ordinance; whether it has ever surveyed this particular sea bed was not established. Coordinates are converted from the degrees-minutes-seconds figure on the Wikipedia article and are approximate to the temple at the point. Reported figures for the height of the cliff conflict badly between sources and are recorded as disputed. All seven Commons images were confirmed through the search and imageinfo APIs and were viewed at thumbnail size before being written here; the two underwater files are honest about being unreadable as architecture and only one of them is used. Nothing operational — access, filming permission, diving permission, boat hire, or whether the bronzes may be filmed at all — has been sought or verified, and local sensitivity about filming at this particular site has not been assessed. Audit, 26 September 2026: the voice and the certain/disputed split were re-checked against Clarke's full text at the Penn Museum and against the Wikipedia article's footnotes. Clarke gives 1624 and the Wikipedia article's 1622 rests on Lach; both are now recorded and the voice says 'the early 1620s'. The priests' burial of the images is Clarke's inference ('must have') and Rasanayagam's statement, and is now narrated as supposed. The levering over the cliff is attested here only through Rasanayagam (1926) as cited by Wikipedia. One finding of the audit brief did not hold up on reading: Clarke does report the disguise, the looting and, hedged with 'probably', the killing, taking them from Balendra, so those have two attestations, not one; they still sit in what_is_disputed because neither has been traced to a seventeenth-century primary text. Rasanayagam's page itself was not read. The line about salt on the bronze every morning was unsourced and has been cut, together with the matching salt clauses in the concept fields. The present-day Gokanna polemic was confirmed from the LankaWeb article of 10 April 2024 and has been added to the risks as a live dispute the voice must never enter.

historical_thread.story:
Koneswaram stands at the end of Swami Rock, the headland that closes Trincomalee bay on the east, and it is one of the Pancha Ishwarams, the five shrines of Shiva that Tamil tradition counts on the island. Its age is not settled and is dealt with separately below. What is not in doubt is that by the early seventeenth century it was a very large and very rich complex: the Portuguese knew it as the Pagoda of Trincomalee and as the Temple of a Thousand Pillars, and a site plan attributed to Fernão de Queyroz describes three monuments on the promontory — 'On the first rise to the summit of the rock was a Pagoda, another at mid-ascent, and the principal one of them all at the highest eminence, visited by a concourse of Hindus from the whole of India.' The chronicler António Bocarro drew monuments at the end of the promontory in his 1635 Livro das plantas.

The date of the destruction is not settled. The main reference account gives 14 April 1622, the Tamil New Year, citing Lach (2022) and Olsen, and names the Portuguese general and governor Constantino de Sá de Noronha; Arthur C. Clarke, writing in 1964 and taking his history from Dr W. Balendra, gives 'the Hindu New Year's Day, 1624'. Both dates are recorded and neither is preferred. What happened on the day reaches this record through two channels only. Clarke, from Balendra, says that Portuguese soldiers disguised as priests mingled with the worshippers, waited until the New Year crowds had followed a procession down the hill, and that then 'the plundering started; probably all those left in the temple were killed, and in a few hours the accumulated treasure of almost two thousand years was looted.' The reference account's statements that soldiers disguised as Iyer priests entered and looted the temple, that the structure was pushed over the edge into the sea, and that fleeing priests buried some of the statues all rest on one cited work, C. Rasanayagam's Ancient Jaffna (1926), p. 378. Clarke does not say how the building reached the sea; he describes its ruins scattered on the sea bed below. Of the burial he writes only that the priests 'must have seized the most sacred images and buried them' — an inference from where the bronzes were later found, not a report. None of this has been checked here against a seventeenth-century Portuguese or Tamil primary text. Temple stones and carved pillars were taken for the fort built on the same headland. The destruction of the three monuments on the rock is given as running from 1622 to 1624, the last pagoda falling in 1624. Between roughly 1630 and 1689 a temple was built at Thampalakamam, inland, to house processional images that had been got away, and it holds them still. No ceremonies were permitted on the rock under Dutch rule; under the British pilgrims returned, and by the mid-nineteenth century a single standing pillar from the old mandapam on the bare summit was the focus of observance. A photograph of that pillar on the empty rock was taken in 1870.

In 1950 the Urban Council of Trincomalee was digging for a water well about five hundred yards from the temple site and met metal about a yard below the surface. Arthur C. Clarke, writing in 1964 and drawing on Dr W. Balendra, who had been central to the rebuilding, records that the digging produced the statues of three Hindu gods, 'more than a hundred pounds' weight of gold and copper alloy', handed over to the authorities, and that further enquiry showed two more statues had been unearthed some months earlier, he does not say where, without the Archaeological Commission or the local authorities knowing; Balendra's own brochure says only that 'Persistent search was made for these finds… and they were ultimately handed over to the Chairman of the Committee appointed to restore the temple.' The standard reference account names five bronzes of gold and copper alloy, believed tenth century: a seated Shiva as Somaskanda, Shiva as Chandrasekhar, Parvati, the goddess Mathumai Ambal and Ganesha. They were taken in procession around the region and reinstalled. Clarke calls them 'among the finest examples of Hindu bronze sculpture known to exist' and the seated Shiva 'a masterpiece'. A restoration committee rebuilt the temple from 1952, and the old images were reinstalled amid opening ceremonies on 3 March 1963; the gopuram dates from the same year and the colossal open-air Shiva was rebuilt in 2018. A three-day procession has followed Maha Sivarathri every year since 1951, the year after the bronzes came up.

In 1956 the writer Arthur C. Clarke and the photographer and diver Mike Wilson were skin-diving about two hundred yards off the headland when they realised that the sea bed under them was not natural. In Clarke's words: 'Huge blocks of stone were scattered in every direction and, though overgrown with weeds and barnacles, many had a curiously artificial appearance… The capital of a stone doorway, badly eroded but perfectly recognizable, lay in the jumbled chaos of rocks. Beside it was a broken column, its square ends bearing on each face a lotus-petal design not unlike the Tudor Rose.' He records that the water where they were diving was 'nowhere more than fifteen feet deep, and most of the broken masonry lay only about five feet below the surface', and that no full-scale investigation was ever carried out because it would have needed heavy lifting gear. The findings went into Clarke's 1957 book The Reefs of Taprobane; elsewhere he calls the battered stonework at the foot of the rock probably the most photographed underwater ruins in the world. Wikipedia states that Wilson and Clarke also retrieved the Swayambhu lingam from the sea floor and that it was reinstalled; a more detailed account says the opposite about the date, that the dives from 1956 onward searched for it without success and that Wilson came on it only in 1962, while the rock was being used as a film location, and that he then took it to the temple where it was enshrined.

The temple today is busy and fully in use, with a gopuram, a courtyard sequence of shrines, a colossal seated Shiva in the open air, and a twenty-two-day chariot festival in April around the Tamil New Year. The cliff drops sheer into the sea and a vertical cleft, called Ravana's Cleft or Lovers' Leap, is split through it and is best seen from a boat. The headland is inside Fort Frederick, which remains a Sri Lanka Army post, and the road to the temple passes a checkpoint. The sea below is an established recreational dive site.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
The concept asks whether the thing a name points at and the name itself are one item or two, and this site ran that question as an experiment for more than three hundred and twenty years without meaning to.

Take the bronze seated Shiva. Before the early 1620s it stood in a shrine and was addressed by a name every day. From then, on the accounts' supposition that it was buried at the destruction, it lay about a yard under the ground, five hundred yards away, and for three centuries nobody in the world knew where it was or said anything to it — while the name it had carried went on being used continuously by people who had no idea the metal existed. In 1950 a council looking for water met it as resistance in a hole, and the first descriptions of it in the record are of an object: metal, a yard down, three of them, better than a hundred pounds' weight of gold and copper alloy, handed to the authorities. Then it was carried round the district and put back in a shrine, and in 1963 it was being addressed by a name again. Four situations. One alloy. The sources' apparatus is not being applied to that history; the history is a worked example of the apparatus. A name-concept is the name that designates something, and the meaning it raises is a separate item that lives in whoever hears the word; the sources are explicit that even the sound and the name are two different things, the sound being ultimately real and the name not. And they sort names into six kinds according to how the name stands to the basis it rests on — a classification that only makes sense if the name and the basis are already being counted separately. Here they were separated physically, by three hundred years of earth, and then rejoined.

The second half of the binding is what the object is made of, and the site provides that too, in two places at once. Bronze is an alloy: it exists because of heat, and the sources define materiality precisely as what is struck and altered by opposing conditions such as cold and heat. Three centuries in soil are exactly that definition being satisfied, continuously, and none of it has any relation whatever to what the object was being called at the time. Under the water, the same point is available in stone: the accounts say the building went over the cliff, and its blocks have been lying at about five feet ever since, and a squared face down there is a worked and manufactured thing with nothing on it, and nothing in it, to say what it was ever called. The sources put squareness itself on the concept side — the ultimates are not lumps like stones or clods of clay but forces, and have no roundness or squareness of their own — so the film's payoff shot is a cut edge that the books have already said is ours.

What makes the location right rather than merely convenient is that the argument does not depend on the politics of what happened, and would be identical if the burial had been an accident. That is also the discipline the site demands. The film records the layers: a temple destroyed by a colonial power on a particular date, stone taken for a fort, metal supposed to have been put in the ground, metal found by people looking for water, metal returned. It ranks none of them, assigns none of them and mourns none of them, and it does not adjudicate what the name refers to — the C084 digest's own bar is that a film must never tell a participant that the name they use is wrong, and a film that concluded 'it was only metal' would have broken it in the last line.
what_is_certain: Koneswaram is a Shaiva temple standing at the end of Swami Rock, the cliff headland east of Trincomalee town, inside Fort Frederick, and is counted among the Pancha Ishwarams of Shiva on the island.

The shrine was attacked and destroyed by the Portuguese on the Tamil (Hindu) New Year in the early 1620s; the Portuguese called it the Temple of a Thousand Pillars, and the main reference account names Constantino de Sá de Noronha as the commander. The year is disputed: see what_is_disputed.
Temple stones and carved pillars were used in the construction of the fort on the same headland.
A temple was built at Thampalakamam, inland, in the seventeenth century to house processional images saved from the destruction, and images remain there.

In 1950 the Urban Council of Trincomalee, digging for a water well about five hundred yards from the temple site, recovered buried statues of the original shrine, of gold and copper alloy and believed to be of the tenth century CE; the standard account names a seated Shiva as Somaskanda, Shiva as Chandrasekhar, Parvati, the goddess Mathumai Ambal and Ganesha. They were taken in procession around the region and reinstalled at the temple.

Arthur C. Clarke's signed 1964 account states that the workmen came on metal about a yard below the surface, that the digging produced three statues comprising 'more than a hundred pounds' weight of gold and copper alloy', that two other statues had been unearthed some months previously without the Archaeological Commission or the local authorities knowing (he does not say where), that the statues were found about five hundred yards from the temple, and that five statues then stood in the new temple, the seated Shiva, which he dates 'from about the 10th century A.D.' — a stylistic attribution — being regarded as a masterpiece.

In 1956 Clarke and Mike Wilson, diving about two hundred yards off the headland, found the sea bed strewn with huge blocks 'overgrown with weeds and barnacles', including the eroded capital of a stone doorway and a broken column whose square ends bore a lotus-petal design on each face. Clarke records the water as 'nowhere more than fifteen feet deep' with most of the broken masonry 'only about five feet below the surface', and that no full-scale investigation was ever made. The findings were published in The Reefs of Taprobane (1957).

A restoration committee rebuilt the temple from 1952 and the old images were reinstalled amid opening ceremonies on 3 March 1963; the gopuram dates from 1963 and the colossal open-air Shiva figure was rebuilt in 2018.

An annual three-day procession has followed Maha Sivarathri every year since 1951, following the rediscovery of the bronzes in 1950, and a twenty-two-day chariot festival runs in April around the Tamil New Year.
A vertical cleft, called Ravana's Cleft or Lovers' Leap, is split through the headland and is clearly visible from the sea.
The temple and its environs are inside Fort Frederick, which is occupied by the Sri Lanka Army as a base; visitors reach the temple through the fort.

The sea below the rock is an established recreational dive site, with reported depths of about five to twenty-four metres, a season of about April to September and reported visibility of fifteen to twenty-five metres.
what_is_disputed: The year of the destruction. The Wikipedia article 'Conquest of Koneswaram Temple' gives 14 April 1622 (Tamil New Year's Day), citing Lach (2022), p. 90, and Olsen, and describes the three monuments on the rock as destroyed between 1622 and 1624, the last pagoda falling in 1624. Arthur C. Clarke, writing in 1964 and taking his history from Dr W. Balendra, dates the attack to 'the Hindu New Year's Day, 1624', and other popular accounts follow 1624. Both dates are recorded and neither is averaged or preferred; the narration says 'the Tamil New Year, in the early 1620s' and says that the accounts do not agree on the year.

The disguise, the looting and the killing. Earliest attestations reached: C. Rasanayagam, Ancient Jaffna (1926), p. 378, which the reference account cites for soldiers disguised as Iyer priests entering and looting the temple; and Clarke (1964), from Dr W. Balendra, who says soldiers 'disguised as priests mingled with the worshippers', that 'probably all those left in the temple were killed' — his own hedge — and that the treasure was looted. Neither has been checked against a seventeenth-century Portuguese or Tamil primary text. An earlier version of this record said the detail descends from seventeenth-century Portuguese and Tamil chronicle tradition; that could not be sourced and has been withdrawn. The narration says 'the accounts say', and does not mention the killing.

That the building was levered or pushed over the cliff into the sea. The only attestation reached is Rasanayagam (1926), p. 378, as cited by the reference account. Clarke describes the ruins of a great building scattered on the sea bed below the headland but says nothing about how they came to be there. The narration says 'the accounts say'.

That priests buried some of the images at the destruction. Clarke writes that the priests 'must have seized the most sacred images and buried them where they hoped they would not be discovered' — an inference from where the bronzes turned up in 1950, not a report of the event; the reference account's 'fleeing priests resorted to burying some of the temple's statues' rests on Rasanayagam (1926), p. 378. The narration says 'the accounts suppose'.

How many bronzes, and how they came up. Wikipedia names five figures recovered by the Urban Council in 1950. Clarke, much closer to the event, says the well-digging produced three and that two more had come out months earlier without the authorities being told; another heritage account describes three upside-down statues from a public well. The count, the sequence and the circumstances all differ, and the narration follows Clarke because he is the earliest and the most specific. Clarke does not say where the two earlier statues were found, and the narration no longer says they came from the same ground.

The lingam. One reference account states that Wilson and Clarke retrieved the Swayambhu lingam from the sea bed, which reads as 1956. A detailed account of Wilson's diving says the 1956 dive and those of following seasons searched for it without success, and that he came on it only in 1962 while the site was being used as a film location, after which it was taken to the temple and enshrined. The 1956 date for the lingam is not safe and the film does not use it.

The temple's age and origins. A seventeenth-century Tamil inscription chronicle, the Konesar Kalvettu, gives circa 1580 BCE. Paul E. Pieris argued in 1917 that this was one of five recognised Ishwarams on the island predating the sixth century BCE. S. Pathmanathan and others date the recorded history to around 300 CE on the Vayu Purana. The Yalpana Vaipava Malai connects the figure of Vijaya and his followers to repairs of the five Ishwarams, and a prince called Kulakottan is credited with a major renovation; some scholars read the Kulakottan narrative as mythical or as conflating later figures. None of this is settled, the film settles none of it, and no antiquity claim is narrated as glory.

Competing claims about the site itself. Since the 1950s some Sinhala Buddhist writers have held the headland to have been the site of the Gokanna Vihara, citing the Mahavamsa's account of Mahasena destroying temples to a deity at Gokarna and building viharas there, and Senarath Paranavitana's reading of a thirteenth-century Sanskrit donative inscription in Grantha Tamil script recording Codaganga's landing at Gokarna in 1223. The identification of Gokarna with this headland, and what follows from it, are contested. A Buddhist vihara stands on the same headland today. The dispute is live, not historical: polemics continue in print, for example a LankaWeb article of 10 April 2024 arguing that there was no Hindu kovil on the headland but the Gokanna vihara. The film records that the claims exist and are contested and adjudicates nothing.

The height of the cliff. Sources give 400 feet (120 metres) 'directly into the sea', 350 feet above sea level for the cleft, and 167 feet for the promontory; dive descriptions put the underwater wall at about twenty-four metres. These cannot all be right and no figure is used in the narration.

Whether the bronzes now in worship are exactly the objects recovered in 1950, and whether any of them has been dated other than by style; Clarke's 'about the 10th century' is a stylistic attribution, which is why the narration says 'believed to be about a thousand years old'. Metallurgical dating is reported for the presiding image at the Thampalakamam temple, not for these.

Clarke's repeated 'three thousand years' of veneration, which he himself attributes to local legend, and his description of the underwater stonework as probably the most photographed in the world. Neither is evidence and neither is used.

The double-fish Pandyan insignia and the prophetic inscription about 'the coming of the Franks', now at the fort entrance. The stone exists; the translation, the dating and the circumstances of its discovery come through later retelling and are not established, and the film does not use it.

unknowns: No permission, temple contact, fixer, boat or dive operator has been sought or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.

Whether the bronzes may be filmed at all should be treated as doubtful and probably refused. Photography inside shrines at this temple is frequently prohibited and photography during puja should be assumed refused. The film is written so that the figures are described and never shown, and a refusal costs it nothing it depends on.

Whether the temple and the community would welcome a film of this kind at this site has not been assessed at all, and it is a real consideration entirely separate from any permit. If the answer is no there is no version worth making.

Drone clearance should be treated as very probably refused. The headland carries an army base, the town is a major naval station, any flight needs Civil Aviation Authority registration and Defence Ministry clearance, and military installations are no-fly. No beat in this film requires an aerial: the wide material comes from a boat and the high material from the cliff top.

Whether diving over the submerged stone can be permitted, and by whom, is unknown and is the single permission the film's payoff depends on. Recreational diving on this reef is routine, but the sea bed is an archaeological context and the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund's Maritime Archaeology Unit are the authorities for it. Whether the unit has ever surveyed this particular site was not established.
Safety at the foot of the cliff — surge, the state of the bottom, boat handling close in — has not been assessed and is a separate question from permission.

How much cut masonry is currently exposed rather than sanded over or overgrown, and whether any worked face is legible on camera, is unverified. The two Commons underwater frames show blocks so overgrown that no architecture reads, and Clarke's description dates from 1956.
Which parts of the fort are closed, and whether a route can be planned that never frames a uniform, a gate or a closed area, can only be settled on the ground.
Whether filming from a boat close inshore under a military headland, in a naval town, requires its own clearance is unknown and should be assumed to.
Whether the last beat's single sentence about the fourth reality survives an expert check on wording; the C002 digest asks for one before any narration touches it.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and is Chathura's to confirm or reject, and the historical detail supporting it is desk research from published reference sources and one signed 1964 first-hand account, separated into what is certain and what is disputed; every operational detail is unverified. No scene or shot is decided here; the sequence is a shape for the film, not a shot list.
